idiom_name: abstract class with a final-by-default skeleton + protected abstract steps and open hooks
implementation_notes: Kotlin members are final by default, so the skeleton is non-overridable unless it is explicitly opened - the guarantee costs no keyword, the inverse of Java - and the steps are `protected abstract` (required) or `protected open` with a default body (hooks). Interfaces may also carry bodies (compiled to JVM default methods, as the Kotlin interfaces documentation explains), so a stateless skeleton can live on an interface; the abstract-class form is still needed when the algorithm reads constructor state or must initialise before the first step runs.
pitfalls: Marking the skeleton `open` - or forgetting `final` on an override - re-opens the algorithm, and an overriding member is itself open by default, so a hook that must stay closed needs `final override`.
Calling an open member from the abstract class's init block or constructor dispatches before the subclass property initialisers have run.
A subclass may widen a protected hook to public on override, exposing the step to clients; keep step visibility part of the documented contract.
